title: Retail investor behavior and social media signals: exploring attention dynamics
venue: Journal of Economics, Finance and Administrative Science
tldr: Social media influencer attention increases stock investment propensity by 17.2% in a four-country OECD sample, but digital financial literacy moderates this effect heterogeneously across national contexts.
problem_and_motivation: Little is known about the mechanisms through which social media recommendations capture the attention of individual investors and shape their willingness to participate in equity markets. Existing literature relies on single-country studies.
approach: Used microdata from the OECD/INFE 2023 International Survey of Adult Financial Literacy covering 6,865 individuals across Brazil, Finland, the Philippines, and Saudi Arabia.
Applied logistic regression with country fixed effects.
Constructed a PCA-based digital financial literacy index.
Applied propensity score matching with nearest-neighbor and Mahalanobis distance methods.
Tested interaction effects between attention and digital financial literacy across country subsamples.
findings: num: 17.2% increase in stock investment probability from social media influencer attention in pooled sample (p < 0.01).
num: 28.1% marginal effect of attention on stock investment in Finland, the highest among all countries.
num: 18.3% marginal effect in the Philippines, remaining significant across all model specifications.
num: In the Philippines, attention x DFL interaction is negative and significant (coefficient -0.148, p < 0.01).
num: Saudi Arabia shows positive interaction between attention and DFL (coefficient 0.0787, p < 0.01).
num: After 2SRI correction, influencer attention remains significant at 1% level.
num: PSM results show treated individuals invest at 32.1% versus 21.8% for controls.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: Provides cross-country empirical evidence on how social media influencer attention drives retail stock market participation. Introduces a PCA-based digital financial literacy index and demonstrates heterogeneous moderating role across countries.
directly_justifies: Social media influencer attention raises stock investment probability by 17.2% in a pooled four-country sample.
Digital financial literacy does not uniformly buffer against social media influence on investment decisions.
The Philippines exhibits a negative interaction between digital financial literacy and attention-driven investment.
Finland shows the highest attention effect (28.1%) despite being a high-literacy country.
limits: Self-reported data may introduce reporting and inference biases.

limitations: Cross-sectional design prevents causal inference about whether attention predicts investment over time.
The influencer recommendation question was newly introduced in the survey, limiting longitudinal comparisons.
Results are based on self-reported data from only four countries.
No measurement of attention intensity, platform specificity, or content characteristics.
remember_this: Social media influencer attention raises stock investment probability by 17.2% in a pooled four-country OECD sample.
Digital financial literacy moderates attention-driven investment heterogeneously: negatively in the Philippines, positively in Saudi Arabia.
Finland exhibits the highest attention effect at 28.1% despite being a high-literacy context.
The study uses 6,865 observations from Brazil, Finland, the Philippines, and Saudi Arabia.
